claim: Myeloid, T, and NK cells are key players in the elimination phase of cancer immunoediting.
source: Myeloid, T, and NK cells are key players in the elimination phase of cancer immunoediting, also referred to as cancer immunosurveillance.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data in this manuscript.

claim: The role of B cells and NAbs in cancer immunosurveillance has been overlooked.
source: However, the role of B cells and NAbs, which are present prior to the encounter with cognate antigens, has been overlooked.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of the field, supported by the subsequent discussion of literature gaps.

claim: Cancer models using muMT mice display a similar tumor burden as their wild-type counterparts.
source: Cancer models using muMT mice display a similar tumor burden as their wild-type (WT) counterparts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: IgHELMD4 mice show a three- to fivefold increase in tumor burden relative to WT mice.
source: However, using two other B cell-deficient mouse models (IgHELMD4 and CD19creDTA), we show a three- to fivefold increase in tumor burden relative to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CD19creDTA mice show a three- to fivefold increase in tumor burden relative to WT mice.
source: However, using two other B cell-deficient mouse models (IgHELMD4 and CD19creDTA), we show a three- to fivefold increase in tumor burden relative to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: B cells and their innate natural antibodies are critical for the detection and elimination of neoantigen-expressing cells.
source: In addition, using an unconventional, non-cancer-related, immune neoantigen model where hypoxic conditions and cell clustering are absent, we provide evidence that B cells and their innate, natural antibodies (NAbs) are critical for the detection and elimination of neoantigen-expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: muMT mice display significantly enhanced type 1 interferon-producing plasmacytoid dendritic cells compared to WT mice.
source: Finally, we find that muMT mice display anti-tumor immunity because of an unexpected compensatory mechanism consisting of significantly enhanced type 1 interferon (IFN)-producing plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), which recruit a substantial number of NK cells to the tumor microenvironment compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2A and 3A.

claim: pDCs in muMT mice recruit a substantial number of NK cells to the tumor microenvironment compared to WT mice.
source: Finally, we find that muMT mice display anti-tumor immunity because of an unexpected compensatory mechanism consisting of significantly enhanced type 1 interferon (IFN)-producing plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), which recruit a substantial number of NK cells to the tumor microenvironment compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Diminishing the compensatory pDC-IFN-NK cell mechanism in muMT mice results in a three- to fivefold increase in tumor burden compared to WT mice.
source: Diminishing this compensatory pDC-IFN-NK cell mechanism revealed that muMT mice develop a three- to fivefold increase in tumor burden compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NAbs are part of an early defense against microorganisms, dying cells, and precancerous cells.
source: In summary, our findings suggest that NAbs are part of an early defense against not only microorganisms and dying cells, but precancerous cells as well.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In the elimination phase of cancer immunoediting, T cells and NK cells are the predominant immune cells to recognize cellular abnormalities.
source: T cells and NK cells are the predominant immune cells to recognize these cellular abnormalities (Rao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rao et al., 2019.

claim: Dendritic cells must become licensed through their pattern recognition receptors by either DAMPs or PAMPs to induce antigen-specific effector T cells against neoantigens.
source: To induce antigen-specific effector T cells against neoantigens (as with other foreign antigens), dendritic cells (DCs) must become licensed through their pattern recognition receptors by either DAMPs or pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to Ardavín et al., 2004.

claim: Licensing allows DCs to present neoantigens in an immunogenic fashion to T cells.
source: This licensing allows for DCs to present neoantigens in an immunogenic fashion to T cells (Ardavín et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ardavín et al., 2004.

claim: DAMPs are the designated mediators that license DCs to present neoantigens in an immunogenic fashion to T cells in the elimination phase.
source: Hence, in the elimination phase, DAMPs are the designated mediators that license DCs to present neoantigens in an immunogenic fashion to T cells (Spörri and Reis e Sousa, 2005; Desch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spörri and Reis e Sousa, 2005 and Desch et al., 2014.

claim: Newly transformed cells that just escaped intrinsic suppression mechanisms do not express PAMPs.
source: However, newly transformed cells that just escaped intrinsic suppression mechanisms do not express PAMPs but must be eliminated too.
evidence: This is stated as a logical premise based on biological knowledge.

claim: Male cells are rejected in syngeneic female mice due to the presence of Y chromosome antigens (H-Y antigens).
source: The first observation is the rejection of male cells in syngeneic female mice. This immune rejection is due to the presence of Y chromosome antigens, H-Y antigens, which are perceived as neoantigens to syngeneic female mice (Atif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Atif et al., 2018.

claim: Adoptive transfer of MHC-matched 129Sv female cells into C57BL/6 female mice results in the rejection of 129Sv cells.
source: Adoptive transfer of MHC-matched 129Sv female cells into C57BL/6 female mice results in the rejection of 129Sv cells, and vice versa (Atif et al., 2015; Carmi et al., 2015; Atif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Atif et al., 2015; Carmi et al., 2015; Atif et al., 2018.

claim: The immune response to 129Sv cells in C57BL/6 mice is due to allelic variations outside of the MHC locus.
source: This immune response is due to the allelic variations outside of the MHC locus.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the observed rejection.

claim: Adoptively transferred C57BL/6 male and 129 female cells have normal MHC class I levels and no PAMPs present.
source: Interestingly, what these two models share in common is that the adoptively transferred cells have normal MHC class I levels and no PAMPs present (Sengupta et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sengupta et al., 2006.

claim: NAbs are required for the elimination of neoantigen-expressing cells in a chain-link reaction involving monocytes, CD11c+Irf4-dependent cells, CD4 T cells, and DC1.
source: In both models, we previously demonstrated that NAbs are required for this elimination process in a chain-link reaction: antibody bound neoantigen-expressing cells license tissue trafficking monocytes and CD11c+Irf4-dependent cells to present cell-associated neoantigens to CD4 T cells, which in turn license DC1 via CD40 to cross-present neoantigens and cross-prime CD8 T cells (Atif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Atif et al., 2018.

claim: NAbs are currently thought to have no role in cancer immune surveillance.
source: Currently, NAbs are thought to have no role in cancer immune surveillance.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: A series of widely cited studies found that B cell-deficient muMT mice mount a robust anti-tumor immune response similar to or greater than wild-type mice.
source: In large part, because a series of widely cited studies found that B cell-deficient muMT mice mount a robust anti-tumor immune response similar to or greater than wild-type (WT) (Supplementary file 1) mice.
evidence: This is supported by a reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: At least three other B cell-deficient mouse models show markedly enhanced tumor growth.
source: At least three other, lesser-known models of B cell-deficient mice show markedly enhanced tumor growth (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by a reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: Antibody depletion with anti-CD20 or anti-IgM shows increased tumor growth.
source: Furthermore, other methods for studying the role of B cells, such as antibody depletion with anti-CD20 or anti-IgM, show increased tumor growth, contradicting the muMT findings and suggest that B cells may mediate early anti-tumor immunity (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by a reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: WT and Aicda−/− mice mounted a robust cytolytic response against 129/BL6 cells, resulting in its rejection.
source: At 18 days post-transfer, WT and Aicda−/− mice (a hyper-IgM mouse) mounted a robust cytolytic response against 129/BL6 cells, resulting in its rejection (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: IgHEL mice did not reject the neoantigen-expressing 129/BL6 cells.
source: In contrast, mice lacking an antibody repertoire, IgHEL mice (hypo-IgM), did not reject the neoantigen-expressing 129/BL6 cells (Figure 1A; Muramatsu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and a citation to Muramatsu et al., 2000.

claim: IgHEL mice exhibit normal DC migration from the tissue to the draining lymph nodes.
source: As expected, since IgHEL mice exhibit normal DC migration from the tissue to the draining lymph nodes (Atif et al., 2018), a similar CTL response against OVA-expressing cells was observed when WT and IgHEL mice were immunized with OVA and poly I:C (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Atif et al., 2018.

claim: A similar CTL response against OVA-expressing cells was observed when WT and IgHEL mice were immunized with OVA and poly I:C.
source: As expected, since IgHEL mice exhibit normal DC migration from the tissue to the draining lymph nodes (Atif et al., 2018), a similar CTL response against OVA-expressing cells was observed when WT and IgHEL mice were immunized with OVA and poly I:C (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: muMT mice lack CD19+ B cells.
source: The first was the most popular B cell-deficient mouse model, muMT mice, which lacks CD19+ B cells.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of muMT mice, also shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Greater than 90% of B cells in IgHEL mice are IgM-specific for hen egg lysozyme.
source: The second strain tested was IgHEL mice, where greater than >90% of B cells are IgM-specific for hen egg lysozyme (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CD19creDTA mice have 70–90% less B cells compared to WT mice, predominantly due to the loss of B1 cells.
source: The third strain was CD19creDTA mice, which have 70–90% less B cells, predominantly due to the loss of B1 cells, compared to WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C and a citation to Atif et al., 2018.

claim: IgHEL and CD19creDTA mice showed an approximately three- to fivefold increase in tumor burden compared to WT mice in the B16F10 melanoma model.
source: Both strains are thus B cell-deficient, and both showed an approximately three- to fivefold increase in tumor burden compared to WT mice (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Atif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Similar observations of increased tumor burden in IgHEL mice were made in a spontaneous, chemically induced lung cancer model using urethane.
source: Similar observations were made of a spontaneous, chemically induced lung cancer model, urethane (Figures 1E and-Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The numbers of pDCs were significantly greater in muMT mice compared to WT mice.
source: However, the numbers of pDCs, which are lymphoid in origin (Sathe et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2018; Dress et al., 2019), were significantly greater in the muMT mice compared to WT mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citations to Sathe et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2018; Dress et al., 2019.

claim: pDCs are lymphoid in origin.
source: However, the numbers of pDCs, which are lymphoid in origin (Sathe et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2018; Dress et al., 2019), were significantly greater in the muMT mice compared to WT mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sathe et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2015; Rodrigues et al., 2018; Dress et al., 2019.

claim: PDCs were identified in LNs and spleen by their co-expression of either Ly6C versus Ly6D, or B220 versus SiglecH.
source: PDCs were identified in LNs and spleen by their co-expression of either Ly6C versus Ly6D, or B220 versus SiglecH (Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: B cells only express Ly6D, but not Ly6C or SiglecH.
source: B cells only express Ly6D, but not Ly6C or SiglecH (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All B220+ cells in muMT mice were SiglecH+.
source: Interestingly, all B220+ cells in the muMT mice were SiglecH+, supporting the notion that these cells are not residual B cells in the muMT mice, but instead pDCs (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: B220+SiglecH+ pDCs were observed in the paracortex and medullary region of WT and muMT mice.
source: B220+SiglecH+ pDCs were observed in the paracortex and medullary region of WT and muMT mice (Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A marked difference was the unique clustering of pDCs in muMT mice within the 'absentee B cell zone,' a region adjacent to the subcapsular sinus.
source: However, a marked difference was the unique clustering of pDCs in muMT mice within the 'absentee B cell zone,' a region adjacent to the subcapsular sinus (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The clustering of pDCs in the absentee B cell zone occurred even in the absence of CXCR5 expression on pDCs.
source: This clustering occurred even in the absence of CXCR5 expression on pDCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: pDCs are potent anti-viral and anti-tumor immune cells.
source: Since pDCs are potent anti-viral and anti-tumor immune cells (Mitchell et al., 2018; Poropatich et al., 2020), we hypothesized that in the muMT mice pDCs are compensating for B cells to elicit an anti-tumor immune response.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mitchell et al., 2018 and Poropatich et al., 2020.

claim: pDCs could either promote or suppress tumor progression depending on their activation state.
source: PDCs could either promote or suppress tumor progression depending on their activation state (Mitchell et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mitchell et al., 2018.

claim: IFN-α, expressed by pDCs, is a robust anti-tumor cytokine.
source: IFN-α, expressed by pDCs, is a robust anti-tumor cytokine.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: pDCs are known as type 1 IFN-producing cells, as they produce type 1 IFNs in larger quantities compared to other immune cell types.
source: PDCs are also known as type 1 IFN-producing cells, as they produce type 1 IFNs in larger quantities compared to other immune cell types (Diebold et al., 2004; Dunn et al., 2005; Ito et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Diebold et al., 2004; Dunn et al., 2005; Ito et al., 2005.

claim: There were significantly more pDCs in the tumor microenvironment of muMT mice than WT mice.
source: First, there were significantly more pDCs in the tumor microenvironment of muMT mice than WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: pDCs in the tumor microenvironment of muMT mice expressed significant levels of IFN-α compared to other cells in the surrounding tissue.
source: Second, these pDCs expressed significant levels of IFN-α compared to other cells in the surrounding tissue (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depleting pDCs in muMT mice resulted in a threefold increase in tumor burden and size compared with non-depleted muMT and WT mice.
source: Depleting pDCs in muMT mice resulted in a threefold increase in tumor burden and size compared with non-depleted muMT and WT mice (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Reconstitution of NAbs with naive WT serum in tumor-bearing pDC-depleted muMT mice significantly diminished the tumor growth compared to pDC-depletion alone.
source: Moreover, reconstitution of NAbs with naive WT serum in tumor-bearing pDC-depleted muMT mice significantly diminished the tumor growth compared to pDC-depletion alone (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In WT mice, pDCs in the tumor microenvironment recruit and activate NK cells.
source: In WT mice, pDCs in the tumor microenvironment recruit and activate NK cells (Joao et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2008; Persson and Chambers, 2010; Swiecki et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Joao et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2008; Persson and Chambers, 2010; Swiecki et al., 2010.

claim: Type I IFN signaling has been associated with NK cell-mediated tumor surveillance.
source: In addition, type I IFN signaling has been associated with NK cell-mediated tumor surveillance (Dunn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dunn et al., 2005.

claim: Type I interferons such as IFN-α facilitate anti-tumor immunity through the activation of immune cells such as NK cells and CD8 T cells.
source: Unlike IFN-γ, which directly target tumor cells, type I interferons such as IFN-α facilitate anti-tumor immunity through the activation of immune cells such as NK cells and CD8 T cells (Dunn et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dunn et al., 2005.

claim: Tumor-bearing muMT mice had significantly more NK cells in their tumor microenvironment than WT mice.
source: As anticipated, tumor-bearing muMT mice had significantly more NK cells in their tumor microenvironment than WT mice.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NK cell frequency in the tumors of muMT mice were diminished after pDC depletion.
source: Moreover, NK cell frequency in the tumors of muMT mice were diminished after pDC depletion (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Low concentration of neutralizing antibodies against IFN-α significantly increased the tumor burden in muMT mice but not in WT mice.
source: Indeed, low concentration of neutralizing antibodies against IFN-α significantly increased the tumor burden in muMT mice but not in WT mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Depletion of NK cells in muMT mice resulted in a fivefold increase in tumor burden compared to depletion of NK cells in WT mice.
source: Moreover, depletion of NK cells in muMT mice resulted in a fivefold increase in tumor burden compared to depletion of NK cells in WT mice, suggesting that the pDC-IFN-I-NK cell axis is the main anti-tumor immune mechanism in place for muMT mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The pDC-IFN-I-NK cell axis is the main anti-tumor immune mechanism in place for muMT mice.
source: Moreover, depletion of NK cells in muMT mice resulted in a fivefold increase in tumor burden compared to depletion of NK cells in WT mice, suggesting that the pDC-IFN-I-NK cell axis is the main anti-tumor immune mechanism in place for muMT mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the effect of NK cell depletion.

claim: WT mice display other anti-tumor immune mechanisms since the tumor burden after the depletion of NK cells was not as dramatic as those observed for muMT mice.
source: In contrast, WT mice display other anti-tumor immune mechanisms since the tumor burden after the depletion of NK cells was not as dramatic as those observed for muMT mice (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing NK cell depletion effects in WT and muMT mice.

claim: The compensatory mechanism exhibited in muMT mice derives from the development of pDCs, which are recruited to the tumor microenvironment in significant numbers, secrete high levels of type 1 IFN, and recruit and activate NK cells that promote anti-tumor immunity.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that the compensatory mechanism exhibited in the muMT mice derives from the development of pDCs, which are recruited to the tumor microenvironment in significant numbers, secrete high levels of type 1 IFN, and recruit and activate NK cells that promote anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: NAbs from WT and Aicda mice bind to B16F10 cells.
source: Western blot analysis and IHC imaging showed that NAbs from WT and Aicda mice bind to B16F10 cells, whereas no binding was detected in naive serum derived from IgHEL, Rag2−/−, and muMT mice Figure 4A-C.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and IHC data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: No IgM binding was detected in naive serum derived from IgHEL, Rag2−/−, and muMT mice when incubated with B16F10 cells.
source: Western blot analysis and IHC imaging showed that NAbs from WT and Aicda mice bind to B16F10 cells, whereas no binding was detected in naive serum derived from IgHEL, Rag2−/−, and muMT mice Figure 4A-C.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and IHC data shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: IgHEL mice do not reject 129/BL6 cells.
source: As previously observed, IgHEL mice do not reject 129/BL6 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: WT and IgHEL mice reconstituted with naive WT serum completely rejected the adoptively transferred 129/BL6 cells.
source: In contrast, WT and IgHEL mice reconstituted with naive WT serum completely rejected the adoptively transferred 129/BL6 cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The tumor burden of IgHEL mice given naive WT serum was significantly reduced compared to untreated IgHEL mice but was still higher than in WT mice in the melanoma model.
source: In the melanoma model, the tumor burden of IgHEL mice given naive WT serum was significantly reduced compared to untreated IgHEL mice but was still higher than in WT mice (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: B cells secreting NAbs are critical for detection and elimination of nascent cancer cells unless abnormal compensatory mechanisms develop.
source: Overall, these data support the hypothesis that B cells secreting NAbs are critical for detection and elimination of nascent cancer cells—unless abnormal compensatory mechanisms develop, such as increased tumor infiltration by IFN-I producing pDCs and NK cells in muMT mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: NAbs tag nascent, precancerous cells for clearance, followed by activation of complement, engulfment by C1q secreting interstitial macrophages, surveying monocytes, and NK cell antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
source: These findings are consistent with an innate immune response in which we envision (requiring further investigation) that NAbs tag nascent, precancerous cells for clearance, followed by activation of complement, engulfment by C1q secreting interstitial macrophages (which are present in all tissues) (Gibbings et al., 2017; Leach et al., 2020), surveying monocytes (Jakubzick et al., 2013), and NK cell antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the data, with citations to Gibbings et al., 2017; Leach et al., 2020; Jakubzick et al., 2013.

claim: C1q secreting interstitial macrophages are present in all tissues.
source: These findings are consistent with an innate immune response in which we envision (requiring further investigation) that NAbs tag nascent, precancerous cells for clearance, followed by activation of complement, engulfment by C1q secreting interstitial macrophages (which are present in all tissues) (Gibbings et al., 2017; Leach et al., 2020), surveying monocytes (Jakubzick et al., 2013), and NK cell antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gibbings et al., 2017 and Leach et al., 2020.

claim: muMT mice possess many immune cell abnormalities, such as reduced T cell numbers, an absence of follicular DCs, poor lymphatic development and DC migration, and small spleens.
source: Although muMT mice possess many immune cell abnormalities, such as reduced T cell numbers, an absence of follicular DCs, poor lymphatic development and DC migration, and small spleens (Asano and Ahmed, 1996; Crowley et al., 1999; Angeli et al., 2006; Schreiber et al., 2011), these mice were used to define for the role of B cells in anti-tumor immunity for decades.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asano and Ahmed, 1996; Crowley et al., 1999; Angeli et al., 2006; Schreiber et al., 2011.

claim: Relying on results from a single mouse model delayed the discovery of the fundamental role B cells play in both innate and adaptive anti-tumor immunity.
source: Although this study does not challenge the empirical validity of previous findings in muMT mice, which are reproducible, it highlights that relying on results from a single mouse model delayed the discovery of the fundamental role B cells play in both innate and adaptive anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discrepancies observed between different B cell-deficient mouse models.

claim: pDCs and B cells share a common lymphoid progenitor.
source: pDCs and B cells share a common lymphoid progenitor (Rodrigues et al., 2018; Dress et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rodrigues et al., 2018 and Dress et al., 2019.

claim: The genetic abnormality that makes the progenitor unable to differentiate into B cells in muMT mice may permit differentiation into pDCs instead.
source: The genetic abnormality that makes the progenitor unable to differentiate into B cells in this model may permit differentiation into pDCs instead.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed increase in pDCs in muMT mice.

claim: pDCs normally represent a small fraction of immune cells in the lymphoid compartment in WT mice.
source: As pDCs normally represent a small fraction of immune cells in the lymphoid compartment in WT mice, they may not be present in sufficient numbers to enter into the tumor environment in WT mice.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of pDCs in WT mice.

claim: In muMT mice, pDCs are present in much higher numbers, and this abundance appears to enable sufficient numbers to migrate into the tumor microenvironment to mount an anti-tumor response.
source: In muMT mice, pDCs are present in much higher numbers, and this abundance appears to enable sufficient numbers to migrate into the tumor microenvironment to mount an anti-tumor response.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased pDCs in muMT mice and their presence in tumors.

claim: IgHEL mice developed significantly more tumors than mice deficient in DC1.
source: Previously, we showed that IgHEL mice developed significantly more tumors than mice deficient in DC1, a potent cross-presenting DC (Atif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Atif et al., 2018.

claim: DC1-deficient mice develop more tumors than WT mice.
source: However, DC1-deficient mice develop more tumors than WT mice.
evidence: This is stated as a known observation.

claim: For anti-tumor immune responses, NAbs contribute to both innate and adaptive immunity, whereas DC1 mainly contributes to adaptive immunity.
source: This observation suggests that for anti-tumor immune responses, NAbs contribute to both innate and adaptive immunity, whereas DC1 mainly contributes to adaptive immunity, and in particular the activation of cytotoxic T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of tumor burden in IgHEL and DC1-deficient mice.

claim: A mouse deficient in both innate and adaptive responses against tumors (IgHEL mice) would develop more tumors than a mouse deficient in only adaptive immunity.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising that a mouse deficient in both innate and adaptive responses against tumors (IgHEL mice) would develop more tumors than a mouse deficient in only adaptive immunity.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the roles of NAbs and DC1 in anti-tumor immunity.

claim: B16F10 injections in the skin may develop comparatively more DAMPs by passing the need for NAbs to mount anti-tumor immunity.
source: However, this hypothesis may also depend on the site of tumor development, such as B16F10 injections in the skin may develop comparatively more DAMPs by passing the need for NAbs to mount anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This is a speculative consideration about the role of tumor location.

claim: A complete NAb repertoire is required to identify altered 'self' and initiate the elimination of neoantigen-expressing cells, resulting in anti-tumor immunity.
source: In summary, our findings indicate that a complete NAb repertoire is required to identify altered 'self' and initiate the elimination of neoantigen-expressing cells, resulting in anti-tumor immunity.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Innate immunity is a critical part of cancer immunosurveillance and clearance of precancerous cells.
source: The implication is that innate immunity is a critical part of cancer immunosurveillance and clearance of precancerous cells—in short, that NAbs are the 'keys' that start the 'engine' of both innate and adaptive immune responses (Atif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with a citation to Atif et al., 2018.

claim: NAbs are the 'keys' that start the 'engine' of both innate and adaptive immune responses.
source: The implication is that innate immunity is a critical part of cancer immunosurveillance and clearance of precancerous cells—in short, that NAbs are the 'keys' that start the 'engine' of both innate and adaptive immune responses (Atif et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a metaphorical conclusion drawn from the experimental data, with a citation to Atif et al., 2018.

claim: Cancer elimination begins with an innate immune response, as with other pathogens and injuries.
source: More broadly, our findings indicate that cancer elimination begins with an innate immune response, as with other pathogens and injuries.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Aicda mice B cells are unable to undergo Ig class switch recombination and have only serum IgM in circulation, lacking all other Ig isotypes.
source: Aicda mice (hyper-IgM), B cells are unable to undergo Ig class switch recombination and have only serum IgM in circulation, lacking all other Ig isotypes (Muramatsu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a known characteristic of Aicda mice, supported by a citation to Muramatsu et al., 2000.

claim: In IgHEL mice greater than 90% of IgM-secreting B cells are specific for hen egg lysozyme.
source: In IgHEL mice (hypo-IgM) greater than 90% of IgM-secreting B cells are specific for hen egg lysozyme.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of IgHEL mice.

claim: 129 strain has allelic variations outside of the MHC locus of C57BL/6 strain.
source: 129 strain has allelic variations outside of the MHC locus of C57BL/6 strain.
evidence: This is stated as a known genetic difference between the strains.

claim: B16F10 melanoma cells and LLC1 tumor cells were confirmed free of mycoplasma contamination and the identification was authenticated through STR DNA profiling.
source: The cell lines were confirmed free of mycoplasma contamination and the identification was authenticated through STR DNA profiling.
evidence: This is a statement about quality control procedures for the cell lines used.
